findings.text: He had.
findings.pattern: M12 - echo-compliance (narration one-liner answering the line just spoken)
findings.test: Test 3 (job): nothing new; Corley's next line carries the same fact
findings.reason: Lyriel asks 'Did you hear about the village...?' and a one-line paragraph answers 'He had.' before Corley's next line shows he heard. The paragraph mirrors the dialogue and adds nothing.
findings.fixNote: Delete the paragraph. Lyriel's line runs straight into '"Fire," he said.'

findings.text: It's the load I book, not the man. That's the rule. It's been the rule since my father had the book.
findings.pattern: M5 - dialogue overexplanation (answer + reason stack)
findings.test: Test 4 / dialogue rule: answer + four reasons where one is allowed
findings.reason: Asked for the carters' names, Corley gives the answer ('I don't write it'), a reason ('The yard's paid at the gate'), then three more justifications ending on a family history. One particular reason is the limit. The tail also duplicates the overseer's 'since my father's time' (line 353); see C-R3-1.
findings.fixNote: Delete the three sentences. The line ends: "They give a name, I don't write it. The yard's paid at the gate." Line 473 still recalls the gate payment.

findings.text: Nine loads on the east road, and two thin strokes.
findings.pattern: M8 - interpreter gloss (recap one-liner of facts just given)
findings.test: Test 3 (job): sums up facts already on the page
findings.reason: Cyndia has just read 'Nine since' for the east road, and line 113 already gave the mage's two thin strokes. The one-line paragraph puts the two facts side by side for effect, and the next paragraph's deduction ('So a month of carts showed as a thin stroke...') does the real work.
findings.fixNote: Delete the paragraph. Cyndia's count runs straight into 'So a month of carts showed as a thin stroke...'

findings.text: The mage had got that off a mile-post in a field with her eyes shut.
findings.pattern: M9 - house wit
findings.test: Test 4 (count): 9 house-wit lines in narration, cap 2; restates an on-page image
findings.reason: A mock-diminishing quip that restates where the read came from (the mile-post at the crossing, lines 15-21). M9 has 9 instances in narration against a cap of 2. This one restates an image already on the page and shares its paragraph with a second quip, so it does not survive the cap.
findings.fixNote: Delete the sentence. The paragraph reads: 'So a month of carts showed as a thin stroke, and a summer of them as a blot with a tail. She went looking for a mark that was wrong. She put her finger on the north road...' (with C-M9-2 applied).

findings.text: Sylvanas would very much have liked one of the marks to be wrong.
findings.pattern: M9 - house wit (mock-precise understatement)
findings.test: Test 4 (count): guide-listed quip; two quips in one paragraph
findings.reason: This exact sentence is listed in the mannered guide as house wit. The plan's interiority (she would like the marks not to match) can survive as an action instead of a quip, which is also how her voice sheet ends an argument.
findings.suggestedFix: She went looking for a mark that was wrong.

findings.text: Thirty-one, out of one shed a day's ride from anywhere that mattered.
findings.pattern: M9 - house wit (comparative put-down) on a recap one-liner
findings.test: Test 4 (count): over the M9 cap; restates the count just given
findings.reason: The paragraph repeats Cyndia's count and adds a sneer at the depot's location. The scale point is already carried by the next paragraph ('She had thought, in that village, that she was following one man... She could follow one man.').
findings.fixNote: Delete the paragraph. Corley's 'I know where they all are.' runs into 'She had thought, in that village...'

findings.text: Terenas's boy, with an army and orcs to chase.
findings.pattern: M9 - house wit (dismissive aside restating the line before)
findings.test: Test 4 (count): over cap; restates an image already on the page
findings.reason: The merchants have just said the prince has an army chasing orcs at Strahnbrad; the fragment repeats that with a sneer. Over the M9 cap. Her verdict on the army comes aloud at line 643, where it does work.
findings.fixNote: Delete the fragment. The paragraph ends: 'She turned back to the table and smoothed the sheet flat.'

findings.text: A free carter had bought back his own spoiled flour at a loss, out of the goodness of his heart, the day before four elves came asking.
findings.pattern: M9 - house wit (sarcastic restatement)
findings.test: Test 3 + Test 4: restates line 239; weakest instance of a pattern at 4.5x its cap
findings.reason: Third telling of the buy-back (line 161, then line 239's 'The last four sacks, bought back at more than he'd been paid for them'), now as sarcasm. 'A quip that restates an image already on the page' is always KILL. M9 stands at 9 against a cap of 2 (over 3x), so the weakest excess instance is raised to MODERATE.
findings.fixNote: Delete the paragraph. Line 239's paragraph runs into 'A day, every time.'

findings.text: This was a town's worth of shed.
findings.pattern: M9 - house wit (exaggerated comparison)
findings.test: Test 4 (count): over cap; the description carries the scale
findings.reason: A quip on scale. The sentence before ('She had pictured Corley's shed, larger.') and the description after (three barns, wharf, crane, a beam that could lift a wagon) already show it. Over the M9 cap.
findings.fixNote: Delete the sentence. 'She had pictured Corley's shed, larger.' runs into 'Three long barns stood end to end...'

findings.text: It came out smooth as a ledger line, every name in its column.
findings.pattern: M8 - interpreter gloss (narration labelling the ready answer)
findings.test: Test 3 (job): translates the line the reader just read; duplicated by line 355
findings.reason: The overseer's answer is on the page, and line 355 then states the tell plainly ('he had answered every question before she'd finished asking it'). The plan asks for the ready answer in plain sight without the narration pointing at it. Two glosses for one tell; this one goes.
findings.fixNote: Delete the sentence and join the two halves of his speech: "...since my father's time. If you take the fork past the chapel..."

findings.text: Corley had run at the nose; this one went white.
findings.pattern: M9 - house wit (comparative put-down)
findings.test: Test 4 (count): over cap; 'this one went white' restates line 323
findings.reason: A joke at Corley's expense (his nose ran from a cold, not fear) set beside a restatement of line 323's colourless face. Over the M9 cap, and it restates an on-page image.
findings.fixNote: Delete the sentence. The paragraph ends on 'Of a mage pointing a stick at his heart.', which line 359 picks up ('ask him which fear it was').

findings.text: On clay a loaded wagon cuts deep.
findings.pattern: M5 - maxim
findings.test: Test 4 (count): 4 narration maxims, cap 2; weakest premise, restated two sentences later
findings.reason: Four maxims in narration (lines 281, 377, 479, 528) against a cap of 2. This is the barest of them, a standalone rule of life in the present tense, and line 381 restates it as a particular deduction ('Six loaded wagons on this road after that rain would have cut through the slumped clay'). Lines 281 and 528 survive (see capCounts).

findings.text: A frightened man doesn't pick what to put in the stove. He puts in the shelf. Or he does, if somebody told him what to pick.
findings.pattern: M5 - maxim (with a muddled counter-rule)
findings.test: Test 1 + Test 4: paraphrase contradicts 'He had burned everything'; over the maxim cap
findings.reason: A rule of life followed by a counter-rule. The logic slips: the sentence before says he burned everything, so 'Or he does [pick]' has nothing on the page to stand on, and 'He puts in the shelf' is a bent way of saying he burned the whole shelf. The plain point is that Barov's name went in with the rest, so the burning does not single out Barov, and that either fear or an order did it, which leads into 'And who told him?'.
findings.suggestedFix: He had put Barov's name in with the rest, because he was frightened or because somebody had told him to.

findings.text: Barov's seal on half of it, his factor's name on more, his stores at the Andorhal end of every one.
findings.pattern: M4 - cadence list with a turn (escalating triplet)
findings.test: Test 1 + M4: the cadence's last item overstates Cyndia's count
findings.reason: The rhythm builds half, then more, then every one, and the payoff claims more than the page shows. Cyndia counted Barov on 31 of the 53 slips (line 463), and Jaina said the family holds 'Most of the granaries, I think.' The plan forbids the narration blurring connection into anything bigger, and this cadence does.
findings.suggestedFix: Barov's name was on more than half of them.

findings.text: Sylvanas inked over the mark.
findings.pattern: M12 - echo-compliance
findings.reason: 'Make it heavy.' followed by a one-line paragraph doing exactly that is the guide's own echo-compliance example, with the verb swapped. Line 578 ('The new mark sat black on Ashford...') already shows the result.
findings.fixNote: Delete the paragraph. Jaina's 'Make it heavy.' runs into 'The new mark sat black on Ashford, across the sheet from the bar through Hollow Green.'

findings.text: And at the top of it, a depot swept to the boards the night before they came, a stove crammed full, a man who had his answer ready before she asked the question. Before that, a free carter who bought his own flour back the day before.
findings.pattern: M3 - equative montage (verbless recap of on-page events)
findings.test: Test 3 (job): recaps a list of on-page images
findings.reason: A list of images summing up events the reader has seen (the sweep, the stove, the ready answer, the buy-back: its third recap after lines 239 and 241). It sums up instead of narrating. 'Who told the overseer?' needs only the depot.
findings.suggestedFix: And at the top of it sat the river depot, swept to the boards the night before they came.
findings.fixNote: Replace both sentences with the one-sentence fix. Line 583 ('Who told the overseer?') should begin its own paragraph; it currently has no blank line before it.

findings.text: and anyone with a pair of eyes and a destination would take it.
findings.pattern: M4 - cadence list with a turn (polysyndeton ending on a quip)
findings.test: M4: the polysyndetic list's last item is the payoff
findings.reason: 'wide and pale and well-drained, the King's road, and anyone with a pair of eyes and a destination would take it' runs a polysyndetic list into a wry turn. Polysyndeton is at 15.5 per 10K against a soft cap of 3.9; of the 17 narration sentences with 3+ 'and's, this is the only one that ends on a turn. The B9 logic does not need the tail: Sylvanas states the King's road's features aloud at line 629.
findings.fixNote: Delete the clause and the comma before it. The sentence ends: '...wide and pale and well-drained, the King's road.'

findings.text: brightening, and then it did a thing she had not seen it do before. The light leaned. It crowded to one side of the stone, the staff standing straight under it, and the side it crowded to was the bend.

Chapter 5 closes on a fork, the staff's light leaning toward the bend, and Sylvanas turning onto the bending road. The plan rests the B9 choice on Jaina's read, which she gives in words at line 556.
